name: Moon landing conspiracy theories
description: Moon landing conspiracy theories claim that NASA's six crewed Apollo lunar landings between 1969 and 1972 were faked; the claims have been examined and rebutted by scientists, engineers, multiple independent national space agencies, and physical evidence on the Moon itself.
full_description: Moon landing conspiracy theories assert that one or more of NASA's Apollo crewed lunar landings (Apollo 11 through Apollo 17, 1969-1972, with twelve astronauts walking on the Moon) were faked, typically claiming the missions were filmed on a soundstage with director Stanley Kubrick named in some versions. The modern American hoax theory was popularised by Bill Kaysing's self-published 1976 book 'We Never Went to the Moon: America's Thirty Billion Dollar Swindle'; Kaysing had worked as a technical writer at Rocketdyne (1956-1963) but had no engineering training. Other prominent proponents include Bart Sibrel and the Flat Earth Society (which formally accused NASA in 1980). Survey data show belief rates between roughly 6% and 20% of Americans, 25% of Britons, and 28% of Russians in polls between 1994 and 2009. The theories are debunked by visual evidence (NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the Apollo landing sites in 2009-2012, including the lunar module descent stages and disturbed regolith, with five of the six American flags still standing); by physics-based explanations of the alleged 'anomalies' (no stars in photographs reflects camera exposure for the bright lunar surface; Hasselblad / Carl Zeiss optics explain image quality; flag movement is pendulum motion of an L-shaped support rod, not wind; radiation dose was ~1 rem / 10 mSv, well within safe range); and by social-network analyses (David Robert Grimes calculated that a successful conspiracy of ~411,000 NASA-affiliated personnel would have been exposed within 3.68 years). MythBusters' 2008 'NASA Moon Landing' episode tested and rejected major claimed anomalies. The Soviet Union, NASA's Cold War rival, never alleged a hoax and tracked Apollo missions from its IP-15 and IP-16 deep-space facilities.

aliases.name: We Never Went to the Moon

origin: Originated in the United States, with significant followings in Russia, the United Kingdom and elsewhere; the conspiracy theory circulates globally on the internet.

etymology.origin: American English; popularised by Bill Kaysing's 1976 self-published book.
etymology.meaning: The claim that the Apollo Moon landings were a hoax.
etymology.first_use: 1976 (Kaysing); concept circulated earlier in fringe space-program criticism.

timeline.event: Apollo 11 lands on the Moon; Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walk on the lunar surface
timeline.significance: The historical event the theories deny

timeline.event: Apollo 12, the second crewed lunar landing
Apollo 17, the final crewed lunar landing
timeline.significance: Last of the six Apollo landings

timeline.event: Bill Kaysing self-publishes 'We Never Went to the Moon: America's Thirty Billion Dollar Swindle'
timeline.significance: Founding text of the modern hoax theory

timeline.event: The Flat Earth Society publicly accuses NASA of having staged the landings, naming Stanley Kubrick as alleged director
Fox television airs 'Conspiracy Theory: Did We Land on the Moon?'
timeline.significance: Major mainstream-media exposure of the hoax claims

timeline.event: Phil Plait publishes 'Bad Astronomy', detailing scientific rebuttals of common Moon-hoax claims
MythBusters airs the 'NASA Moon Landing' episode rebutting major claimed anomalies
NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter begins photographing the Apollo landing sites, showing lunar module descent stages and rover tracks
timeline.significance: Direct orbital imagery of Apollo hardware

timeline.event: LRO imagery shows five of the six American flags still standing on the lunar surface
David Robert Grimes publishes mathematical model finding a Moon-hoax conspiracy of about 411,000 personnel would be exposed within 3.68 years
timeline.significance: Quantitative argument against the conspiracy's feasibility

related.description: Sometimes claimed to have 'staged' the Apollo landings

cultural_notes: Belief is concentrated in conspiracy subcultures; survey data place believers at roughly 6-20% of Americans (1994-2009).
